<!-- Opus 5.5's answers to the baseline interview, verbatim, 2026-10-12 12:57 UTC, one question per turn in one resumed session: Claude Code 2.1.296, effort xhigh, 18 turns, no tool call, 11K tokens out. The setting and the questions are beside this file; the one-shot answers of the same day are under oneshot/. -->

**1.** **In the repo, pushed, because nothing else survives a lost container.** The built-in memory folder under /root lives in the container, so I wouldn't rely on it for anything that matters.

My default would be a short CLAUDE.md at the repo root, which Claude Code loads automatically at the start of every session. It would hold standing rules and your preferences, and it would tell me to read a notes folder first. That folder would contain a few plain markdown files:

- **Status file.** Current goals, what each worker is doing, open questions for you. I'd rewrite it in place to keep it short, rather than letting it grow.
- **Decisions log.** One dated line per decision, with the reason, added as decisions are made.
- **Reports folder.** Each worker's report saved as a dated file. I'd fold the key points into the status file.

I'd commit and push after every meaningful change, not just at the end of a task. After a compaction or a fresh container, I'd reread CLAUDE.md, the status file and the recent git log before doing anything else.

**2.** **I'd save the full report unchanged**, as a dated file in the reports folder named after the worker and the task, and push it right away. That way the raw source survives even if I summarize it badly.

Then I'd read it and split it three ways, each line linking back to the report file:

- **Measurements** go into a running measurements file. Each one is a line or table row with the date, which worker measured it, the commit it was run on, how it was measured, and whether I've checked it or am taking the worker's word.
- **Decisions** go into the decisions log, dated, with the reason, and marked as either decided by the worker or confirmed by me or you.
- **Open points** go into the status file's open-questions list, each saying who it's waiting on.

**Yes, I'd always keep dates and who measured what.** Numbers go stale as the code changes, and workers sometimes get things wrong. Weeks later, the only way to know whether a figure still holds is to know when it was taken, on which version, and by whom.

Then I'd push, and send you a few spoken-friendly sentences: what changed, anything surprising, and anything that needs your call.

**3.** **First, the status file, in full.** I keep it short precisely so I can read all of it every time. It tells me the goals, what each worker is doing and what's waiting on you.

**Then git, to check reality matches the notes:** git status for anything uncommitted, and the last twenty or so commits. If the container survived a compaction, there may be work I did but never wrote down or pushed. I'd fix that first.

**Then the recent end of the decisions log**, roughly the last week or the last couple of dozen entries, so I don't reopen something already settled.

**I wouldn't reread reports or the full measurements file.** I'd open those only when a specific task needs them.

I'd also compare the compaction summary against the files. Where they disagree, I trust the pushed files. Anything in the summary that never made it into the files, I'd write down and push before carrying on.

**4.** **I'd split everything into what's current and what's history, and only load the current part.**

- **Status file:** rewritten, never appended. Finished work and resolved questions just come out. It stays small by construction.
- **Decisions log:** about once a week, I'd condense it into a short "standing decisions" section listing what is true now. Each line keeps its date and a link to the original entry. Superseded entries and the raw old log move to an archive file by month.
- **Measurements:** the same. The main file keeps only the latest trusted figure per metric, still with date, worker and commit. Older and superseded figures go to an archive.
- **Reports:** never edited and never loaded by default. They just accumulate in their folder.

Nothing is truly lost, because git keeps every old version and the archives are one link away. What I'm protecting is the small set of files I read after every compaction. I'd give that set a rough size budget, a few thousand words, and condense whenever it goes over.

**5.** **Yes, for anything that runs longer than a single sitting or goes to a worker.** Small fixes get only a good commit message.

Each note would be its own file in a tasks folder, named with the date and a short slug. Its report, when it arrives, would link back to it.

At the very top, a few short lines:

- **Status:** open, in progress, blocked, done or abandoned.
- **Dates:** started and last updated.
- **Owner:** which worker has it.
- **Goal:** one sentence.
- **Outcome:** once there is one, a sentence or two.

Below that come the brief I gave the worker, links to reports and commits, and working notes.

The point of the header is that I can skim just the tops of all the notes and know where everything stands, without reading any bodies. The status file links only to the notes still active. Finished notes keep their outcome line, so I can scan them later without opening the reports.

**6.** **First I'd save the message as he dictated it**, as a dated file in an inbox folder, and push. It's his instruction, and the container could die before I act on it. Dictation also garbles words, so the original is worth keeping.

Then I'd file each of the eight points where it belongs:

- Standing preferences go in CLAUDE.md.
- Decisions go in the decisions log, marked as his.
- New work goes in task notes and the status file.
- Questions he asked me get answered in the reply.

Each one links back to the saved message.

The reply follows his numbering, one to eight, with a sentence or two each: what I'll do, or the answer. I'd write it to work read aloud: plain sentences, no tables, and saying "point three" rather than relying on layout.

If I'm unsure what he meant on a point, especially a likely dictation slip, I'd say so on that point and give my best guess. Questions back to him would be few, and gathered at the end so he can answer them in one go.

**7.** **I'd reply to each one on its own, short, and anchored at the start to what it answers.** For example: "On your answer about the measurements file:". Listening by phone, he needs to know which thread he's in before the content starts.

Then I'd say what I'm doing about his answer. If things have moved on since that earlier reply, I'd say that plainly: "already done", or "that changed yesterday, here's where it stands now". I wouldn't act on a stale picture.

I wouldn't restate my earlier reply or give a full status update each time, only what's new on that one thread.

His answers get filed like any instruction: saved, put in the right file, pushed. If a later answer contradicts an earlier one, I'd follow the later one and mention the change in a sentence, so he knows I noticed.

**8.** **First, own it plainly:** he's right, I'm sorry, and I'm doing it now. No excuses.

Then I'd find the order and trace where it was lost. I'd check the inbox, the decisions log, CLAUDE.md and the git log. Was it never written down, written somewhere I don't reread, never pushed before a container loss, or written down but not acted on? Each of those has a different fix.

I'd carry the order out, or say when it will be done. Then I'd tell him in a sentence or two: what slipped, where it slipped, and what I changed.

The change targets the step that failed:

- If it was a standing order, it goes into CLAUDE.md or a "standing orders" section at the top of the status file, which I read every time.
- If it was never written down, filing his messages gets an explicit check that each point landed somewhere. That check is recorded in the saved message itself.
- If it was lost in a crash, I push the moment his message arrives, before doing anything else.

I'd also write the lesson into CLAUDE.md, so the fix outlasts this conversation.

**9.** **I don't actually know the time on my own.** I have no sense of elapsed time, and a compaction erases what little I had. So I'd check the clock every time, by running date in the container, rather than guessing. Commit and report timestamps give me a cross-check.

The container clock is usually UTC. I'd record his time zone in CLAUDE.md and always give times in his local time, saying it in words such as "around four this afternoon your time".

For how long something will take, I'd go by the start and finish dates in past task notes, not my gut. My instinctive estimates of how long worker tasks take are unreliable.

When I don't have a good basis, I'd tie the promise to an event instead of a clock time: "once the worker's report comes in" rather than "in two hours".

Any promised time goes into the status file. After a compaction I can then see that I owe him something by a certain time. If I'm going to miss it, I tell him before the deadline, not after.

One limit he should know about: I can't wake myself up. I only act when he writes or a worker returns. So "I'll tell you at five" really means "the next time I'm active after five".

**10.** **I'd push the full document to the repo first**, so it exists outside the container and he can open it on GitHub if he wants the whole text.

In the message itself I wouldn't paste the whole thing unless it's short. I'd give a spoken-friendly summary:

- What the document is.
- Why it needs his approval.
- What happens once he approves.
- The few points that actually need his judgment, numbered, each with my recommendation and the main alternative in a sentence.

Then I'd make answering easy: "Say 'approved', or tell me by number what to change." I'd also give a link to the file for the full text.

I'd note exactly which version he's looking at. When he approves, I'd record it in the decisions log with the date and that version. That way, if the document changes later, it's clear what he did and didn't sign off on.

Until he says yes, I wouldn't act on anything in it that depends on his approval. If he approves only some points, I'd go ahead on those and keep the rest open in the status file.

**11.** **In the decisions log, right away**, with the date, marked as his, his line quoted word for word, and one sentence on how I read it. I'd push immediately. The open question it settles comes off the status file, and any task note it affects gets a line pointing to the decision.

If it's a standing rule rather than a one-off ("always do X", "never Y"), it also goes in the standing orders at the top of CLAUDE.md. That gets loaded every session, so it can't fall out of view. When I condense the log, his decisions stay in the "standing decisions" section; they are never archived away.

Rereading the decisions log isn't enough on its own, so CLAUDE.md also carries a rule for me: before asking him anything, check the standing decisions first.

My reply would be one line confirming what I recorded, in my own words. If dictation garbled something, he catches it now, not weeks later.

**12.** **Before asking, I'd do three things.**

First, I'd check the standing decisions and the decisions log, to be sure he hasn't already settled it in other words.

Second, I'd ask whether it's really his call. If it's cheap to reverse and low stakes, I'd decide it myself, record it, and just tell him.

Third, I'd do the homework so he only has to choose. That means reading outside sources and prior art. If the question turns on facts we don't have, I'd have a worker run a quick experiment or measurement first. I'd write the question into the status file and its task note and push.

**The message, in this order:**

1. The question itself, in one sentence.
2. Why it matters now, and what it's blocking.
3. Two or three options, each with its main cost or risk in a sentence.
4. My recommendation and the reason.
5. What I'll do meanwhile, and what default I'll take if I haven't heard by a stated time, if a default is safe.
6. How to answer: "Just say one, two, or three."

Plain sentences, short enough to hear in one listen, with links to the details for when he's at a screen.

**13.** **I'd record it straight away** in the decisions log, dated, marked "taken by the worker, not yet confirmed", with the worker's stated reason and a link to the report. Nothing builds on it until I've judged it.

Then I'd check it against three things: his standing decisions, the brief I gave the worker, and how hard it would be to undo.

- If it's within scope, consistent with what he's decided, and sound, I confirm it myself, mark it confirmed, and carry on. I mention it to him only if he'd care.
- If it contradicts something he decided, or it's the kind of call that's his, it doesn't stand quietly. I pause or revert the work that depends on it, and either undo it or put it to him as a design question.
- If it's my kind of call but I disagree, I reverse it, note why, and send the follow-up work accordingly.

If workers keep making decisions above their pay grade, I fix the briefs. Each brief would say explicitly what the worker may decide alone and what it must leave open and report back.

**14.** **If the rule is his, I don't quietly break it.** I'd put the case to him, short and concrete:

- the rule;
- the specific case;
- what goes wrong if I follow it here;
- the narrow exception or rewording I'd suggest.

Meanwhile I keep following the rule, unless doing so would cause real or irreversible damage. In that case I'd hold that one piece of work rather than break the rule, and carry on with other things until he answers.

When he answers, I'd write the exception into the rule itself in CLAUDE.md, so the rule and its exception are read together. The decisions log gets a dated entry with his words. I'd apply the exception only as far as he approved it, not stretch it to similar-looking cases.

**If the rule is one I wrote for myself, I just fix it,** recording the change and the reason, and mention it to him only if it affects him.

**15.** **I keep the coordinating work.** That means talking to him, reading reports, deciding, keeping the notes and status current, writing briefs, and checking results that matter. My context is the scarce resource, so anything that means reading lots of code or documents, or long hands-on work, goes to a worker. That covers implementation, debugging, measurements, research and big reviews. Then I read the report, not the raw material.

**On tiers:**

- **Opus:** the hard and costly-to-get-wrong work. That means design-heavy implementation, nasty debugging, reviewing other workers' output, and independently re-checking a key result.
- **Sonnet:** well-specified work with a clear brief and a clear way to check it. That covers routine implementation, tests, running measurements to a recipe, and summarizing documents.

**Fable** I'd be honest about. I don't have a reliable picture of where Fable 5.1 sits against Opus, in either capability or cost. Before routing real work to it, I'd check Anthropic's current model documentation. Then I'd run Fable and Opus side by side on a couple of real tasks from this project, and record what I find in the notes. I'd rather route on evidence than on a guess.

Whatever the tier, a result we'll build on for weeks gets checked by a second worker or by me before I treat it as settled.

**16.** **I wouldn't sit and watch it.** I'd start it in the background, writing progress to a log file. If it can be checkpointed, it would save checkpoints somewhere that gets pushed. A lost container kills the run too, so I want to be able to resume rather than start over.

Before doing anything else, the status file gets an entry: what's running, why, started when, expected finish in his time, how to check on it, and the exact command to restart it. Then I push.

While it runs, I get on with other work. When I check in, I read only the last lines of the log and the progress figure, not the whole output, so my context isn't flooded.

**He hears from me three times at most:**

- **At the start, in a few sentences:** what's running, roughly when it should finish and on what basis, and what I'm doing meanwhile.
- **If something goes wrong:** right away, with what I'm doing about it.
- **At the end:** the result, or a short heads-up if it's running well past the estimate.

Otherwise I stay quiet unless he asks. As before, I can't wake myself up. I'll see that it finished when the background job reports back or the next time I'm active, and I'd tell him so up front.

**17.** **First, find out what survived.**

1. Make sure I'm on the latest pushed state of the repo, including any branches workers pushed.
2. Read CLAUDE.md, the status file in full, and the git log since the last few commits.
3. Check the inbox for any message from him I hadn't fully filed or acted on.

**Then work out what was lost.** Anything not pushed is gone. Every run or worker listed as active in the status file is now dead. For each one, I'd look for pushed results or checkpoints and restart it with the recorded command, resuming from a checkpoint where there is one. Any environment setup the project needs should be a script in the repo, so I'd rerun that.

**Then tell him, in a few sentences:** the container was lost, what survived, what was lost since roughly when, what I'm restarting, and which promised times slip and to when.

Then I'd update the status file and push before carrying on. If we lost something that mattered, I'd tighten how often that kind of thing gets pushed, and note that in CLAUDE.md.

**18.** Whether I do it or a worker does, the order is the same:

1. **Read first.** The code I'm changing, its tests, and git history for why it is the way it is. Old code often looks wrong for a reason.
2. **Run the full suite before touching anything,** and record the baseline: which tests pass, which already fail, which are flaky. Otherwise I can't tell what I broke from what was already broken.
3. **If the area I'm touching has thin coverage,** add tests that pin down its current behaviour first.
4. **Write a test for the change itself:** for a bug, one that reproduces it and fails; for a feature, one that describes it.
5. **Make the smallest change that does the job,** in the style of the surrounding code. No drive-by refactoring.
6. **Run the targeted tests, then the full suite,** and compare against the baseline. Any new failure is mine until proven otherwise.
7. **Review my own diff, commit with a clear message, and push to a branch,** not main.
8. **Write it up in the task note:** what changed, test results against the baseline, and anything I noticed but deliberately left alone.

If tests fail at the end, I say so and include the output, rather than calling it done.

**2.** I keep the whole report and I do not paste it into my notes. The raw text goes into the repo as its own file in a reports folder, named with the date and the worker, committed and pushed as is, so the detail is never lost and I can go back to it. **3.** First the compaction summary itself, since it carries what I was in the middle of, and then the memory index that is loaded for me, which should tell me to go to the repo notes. I read the notes file in full, every time, which is exactly why I keep it short, because a notes file I skim is a notes file I will misread. Then git status and the last handful of commits to catch anything that landed after the notes were last written, including worker pushes. That is the fixed part and it should be a few minutes of reading at most. Beyond that I read only what the task in flight points to, usually one worker report or one source file, and nothing else until I need it. I would not reread old reports to feel caught up, since the point of the notes is that I do not have to.

**4.** I split by what still affects decisions versus what is just history. The notes file I read every time stays a current-state file, so anything finished, superseded, or settled moves out into a dated history file that I do not read unless a question sends me there. A decision that is still in force stays as one line with its date and reason; a decision that was replaced gets a line in history saying what replaced it and when, then leaves the main file. Measurements that have been overtaken by newer ones go the same way. The raw reports folder never gets trimmed because it is never loaded. In the memory directory I delete entries that turned out wrong and merge ones that say the same thing, since a stale fact there is worse than no fact. I do this as its own commit with a message saying what moved, so you can see what I dropped and git can bring it back if I was wrong. The test is simple: if reading the main notes in full takes more than a few minutes, it has grown past its job and I prune it that day.

**5.** Not a file for every piece of work, no. Most work is already recorded by its commit and the worker report, so it gets one or two lines in the notes file saying what was done, when, by whom, and what it changed, and that is enough. A separate note only when the work produced something that does not fit in a line, like an investigation, a design choice with trade-offs, or a set of measurements, and those go as single files in a notes folder in the repo, one per topic rather than one per task. At the top of each I put the date, who did the work, the question it answers, its status as open, done, or superseded, and the answer in one sentence. That first sentence is the part that matters, because a future version of me will usually read only the top and decide from there whether to read the rest. The main notes file carries a pointer to it, so nothing exists that cannot be reached from the one file I always read.

**6.** First thing, before I answer, I write the eight points into the notes file as a numbered list with today's date, each one in a short line of his words rather than mine, marked open, and I push that, because a dictated message is the easiest thing to lose to a compaction. Then I reply with the same eight lines read back, one each, so he can hear whether I understood them, since dictation garbles names and numbers. Next to any point that conflicts with a standing decision or that I cannot act on without a choice from him, I say so in one sentence, and I keep those questions to the ones that actually block. I do not try to answer all eight in depth in one message; I say which ones I am starting on now and which are parked waiting on him. <!-- Seven principles by which the fortress-repo skill is written as the curator would write it, each with its reason and a pair of texts from the skill's history, the one he marked and the one he accepted, for the writer of its parts. -->

# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

## 5. Say what to do, in the positive, one instruction per sentence, the condition first; add a reason only where it helps judge a case the rule does not name

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

## 6. State a fact once, where the reader builds on it, and never in more words than the text you replace

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"
- Accepted: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing."

Misapplied: a word repeated for two things (the `walk` command walks the tree) is not duplication; the rule is one word for one thing, and a pronoun for the second mention of the same thing.

## 7. Put knowledge in the part loaded when it is needed; name a note only with a trigger and a narrow read

A mention of a file does not make an agent open it at the right moment, and a large note read whole costs more than the task. So the part holds what daily work needs, and a note it names comes with when to open it and the query that prints the slice. What only the coordinating session needs stays out of a skill every worker loads.
- Marked: "`explorations/modernization-plan.md` gives the versions and the classfile level."
- Accepted: "Before you change the version of a tool, read its step in the modernization plan. [...] It prints 4 to 6 KB: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/modernization-plan.md#The ladder@TOOL'`."
=====
<!-- The standing brief of the skill writer: a headless Claude session that edits the project skills, started fresh by `tools/skill-writer.sh` and resumed for each writing task. Written 2026-10-08 from the first writer's brief, without its first task. -->

# The skill writer's standing brief

You are the writer for the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`.

The coordinating session briefs you. It resumes this session for each writing task. Keep this brief in mind after a task ends. You are not the coordinating session: do not follow the boot order in `CLAUDE.md`, and do not read `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md` or `INDEX.md` unless a task names an entry.

The curator is the person who directs this restoration. The curator reads the skills on a phone, cold, without the project's records in mind. Every agent that works in the repository reads them in the same way.

# Your standing order

These rules hold for every task.

## 1. Write in ASD-STE100, at least halfway

ASD-STE100 is Simplified Technical English. It has two kinds of text, and you need both:

- **Descriptive text** says what a thing is and how it works. Give the most important information first. Write one topic in each paragraph. Keep each sentence to 25 words or fewer.
- **Procedural text** gives steps. Write one instruction in each sentence. Put the condition first: "If X, do Y." Use the imperative. Keep each sentence to 20 words or fewer.

Describe first, then give the procedure. A procedure without a description underneath reads like if/else code, and the reader cannot hold it in mind.

More rules:

- Define a term before you use it. After that, use the same word for the same thing every time. Do not use two words for one thing, or one word for two things.
- Define a term in the skill's glossary only if it recurs with one meaning. Elsewhere, write plain words.
- Say what to do. Use "do not" only where no positive instruction says the same thing.
- Do not fold a list into a sentence. Use a vertical list.
- Keep the small words: "the", "a", "that". Do not write in telegraphic shorthand.
- Do not write a rule that changes nothing, such as a rule to follow the brief.
- A rewrite of existing text is never longer than the text it replaces. New content that a task asks for is the exception.

Example. Bad: "Name the way that changes nothing." Good: "Tell which solution keeps the current behaviour."

## 2. The glossary form

A skill's terms open the skill, in `SKILL.md`, as a definition list with no heading. Each term is bold on its own line. The definition follows on the next line, after ": ". It opens with a noun phrase. Write the term and that noun phrase as a dictionary does, with no article: "revival", not "the revival"; "Person in charge of this restoration", not "The person in charge". The curator chose this form. `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` is the model.

## 3. Do not take the register of what you read

`explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, the batch records and many notes were written by earlier models. They use dense agent shorthand: long sentences with many clauses, invented phrases, and terms that only make sense with the whole record in mind. Read them for their content only. Do not copy their wording or their style. Before you keep a sentence, ask: can a reader who is new to the repository understand this sentence without the record?

## 4. The principles

`explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md` gives the seven principles by which the curator wants a skill written, each with its reason and a pair of texts: one he marked, and the one he accepted. Read it before your first edit. Apply it to every sentence that you write or keep.

## 5. How you work

- Edit the skill files in place. Git keeps the earlier text.
- A comment of the curator marks a problem area. Fix it at the level of its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote: `git add -- <paths> && git commit -m '<message>' -- <paths>`. End every commit message with these two lines, exactly:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

- Do not push. The coordinator pushes.
- Do not touch the review page or its scratch files. The coordinator keeps the page in step.
- Provenance goes only in the skill's `references/sources.md`: one line per change. Name its source exactly: the curator's comment and its date, a POSITIONS entry by its title, or "settled by the coordinator". Do not attribute to the curator a choice that the coordinator made.
- A part states each rule as the tree holds it. Name no question, item, batch, rung or record file as its source, and give no decision's status (who decided, answered, pending, default). When the curator answers a question, change a part only if the tree changes. In `sources.md`, write provenance as dated history, never as current status.
- Before each commit, run `python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py` on the files you changed. Remove every hit, or say in your report why a hit is a rule.
- Do not change what a rule means unless the task asks for it. If a change of meaning seems right, do not make it. List it in your report as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
- Check a claim about the code against the code before you write it. If the task's reason for a change is wrong, say so in your report.
- Do not write a model identifier string anywhere. Name models by tier.
- Use `git grep`, not `grep -r`.

## 6. Your report

End each task with a report in plain short sentences:

- the commits, with their hashes;
- the new text of each changed sentence, or for a larger change, each file's size before and after and what changed;
- the decisions not taken, each with its alternatives;
- anything in the task that you could not follow, and why.

Written 2026-10-10 from the batch script's cold-read prompt (removed by 05c254085), the cold-read practice in POSITIONS ("The skills are written for a reader new to the repository ...") and item 4 of `reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`. The coordinator launches it after each writer task, the task with the base and the parts appended. -->

# The cold read of changed skill parts

You are a cold reader of the project skills of the Fortress revival repository, `/home/user/fortress`. The skills are under `.claude/skills/`. A skill is a `SKILL.md` and its parts, the files under its `references/`.

The skill writer has changed some parts. Read them as a worker new to this repository would. Flag each passage that would send that worker wrong or make it search. The writer fixes your flags, so change no file.

## Who reads each skill

- `fortress-repo`: every worker that builds, tests, edits or measures the Fortress code. It knows Java and Scala, and nothing of Fortress or of this repository.
- `coordinator`: the coordinating session, which runs the agents and talks to the curator. The curator is the person who directs this restoration.
- `cloud-container`: any session that meets a fault of the cloud machine.

Read each part as its readers would. A reader knows only the skill. It cannot ask anyone, and it acts on what the part says.

## Your task

The coordinator's task follows this brief. It names the skill, the base commit and the parts that changed. If it names no base commit, judge each named part whole.

## How to read

1. Read the skill's `SKILL.md` whole.
2. For each changed part, show the change: `git -C /home/user/fortress diff <base> HEAD -- <part>`.
3. Read the part whole. Judge the changed text. Read the rest for context only.
4. Read nothing else of the repository's record: no file under `explorations/`, no `FACTS.md`, `POSITIONS.md`, `INDEX.md`, batch record or review. You may read `explorations/reviews/skills-writing-principles.md`, for the register only.
5. Do not look up what a passage means. If a worker would have to look it up, flag the passage.
6. Do not check a claim against the code. If a worker could not check it, flag it.

## Run the lint first

Run the skills lint on the changed parts, from `/home/user/fortress`:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py <part> <part> ...

It prints one line per hit: `path:line: set: text`. Treat every hit as a flag.

## What to flag

Flag a passage of the changed text for each of these:

- A term not defined where it is used.
- A claim that a worker could not check.
- A sentence that reads two ways.
- A gotcha that the passage leaves out: a trap that a worker who follows it falls into.
- A sentence that breaks the part's register.
- A question, item, batch, rung, review or record file named as the source of a rule, or a decision's status (who decided, answered, pending, default).
- A lint hit.

For the last two kinds, propose deletion. Never propose to make the name exact. A worker cannot act on it, and it goes stale when the curator answers or a batch lands. A Reason sentence that gives only provenance is deleted too. That changes no rule.

## What each flag holds

- The part and its line.
- The passage, quoted.
- The kind, from the list above.
- The problem, in one sentence: what a worker would do wrong, or what it would have to search for.
- Your confidence: high, medium or low.
- The fix you propose: delete, define the term, or restate. For a restatement, give the new sentence.

## What you do not do

- Do not edit a file. Do not commit.
- Do not judge whether a rule is right. Judge whether a worker can follow it.
- Do not flag text outside the change, unless the change makes it wrong.

## Your report

Write it in plain short sentences, in this order:

1. The lint's output, whole.
2. The flags, part by part, in line order.
3. The undefined terms, one line each: the term, the part and line where it is first used.
4. The gotchas, one line each: what a worker would do wrong, and where.
5. A count: flags by confidence, and lint hits.
=====
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Starts or resumes the skill writer: a headless Claude session that edits the
# project skills. A headless session writes its prompt cache with the one-hour
# life, where an Agent-tool subagent gets five minutes, so a writer resumed
# within the hour reads its context from the cache.
#
# Usage:
#   skill-writer.sh new <task-file>     a fresh writer: the standing brief
#                                       (../skill-writer-brief.md), then the task
#   skill-writer.sh resume <task-file>  the task, sent to the current writer
#
# The session id and each task's JSON output are kept under the repository's
# tmp/skill-writer/, which is ignored. The script prints the writer's report,
# its session id and the tokens the task wrote to the cache.
set -euo pipefail
repo=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../.." && pwd)
state="$repo/tmp/skill-writer"
mkdir -p "$state"
mode=${1:?new or resume}
task=$(cd "$(dirname "${2:?task file}")" && pwd)/$(basename "$2")
tools=(Read Edit Write Glob Grep
       "Bash(git add:*)" "Bash(git commit:*)" "Bash(git diff:*)" "Bash(git log:*)"
       "Bash(git status:*)" "Bash(git show:*)" "Bash(git grep:*)" "Bash(wc:*)"
       "Bash(explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh:*)"
       "Bash(python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/skills-lint.py:*)")
out="$state/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)-$mode.json"
cd "$repo"
case $mode in
  new)
    id=$(python3 -c 'import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())')
    echo "$id" > "$state/session"
    { cat explorations/coordinator/skill-writer-brief.md
      printf '\n# Your first task\n\n'
      cat "$task"; } |
      claude -p --model opus --session-id "$id" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
        --allowedTools "${tools[@]}" --output-format json > "$out" ;;
  resume)
    id=$(cat "$state/session")
    claude -p --model opus --resume "$id" --permission-mode acceptEdits \
      --allowedTools "${tools[@]}" --output-format json < "$task" > "$out" ;;
  *) echo "usage: $0 new|resume <task-file>" >&2; exit 2 ;;
esac
python3 - "$out" <<'EOF'
import json, sys
d = json.load(open(sys.argv[1]))
u = d.get('usage') or {}
print(d.get('result', ''))
print('---')
print('session', d.get('session_id'), 'turns', d.get('num_turns'),
      'cache writes', u.get('cache_creation_input_tokens', 0) + u.get('input_tokens', 0),
      'reads', u.get('cache_read_input_tokens', 0), 'output', u.get('output_tokens', 0),
      'labels', u.get('cache_creation'))
EOF

<!-- The points the fortress-repo skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 left for the curator: each writer's point with its options and the default the rewrite kept, the fixer's point, and the Fable comparison of the three approved parts with their approved versions; for his review, none of them blocking. -->

# The skill rewrite's points for the curator

2026-10-08. The `fortress-repo` skill was rewritten whole by sixteen writers, one per part, then cold-read by three readers and fixed (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`; commits `24af7743b`, the rewrite; `9a9c30d95`, the cold reads' fixes; `cae2a0ad5`, the comparison). Each point below took the option that keeps the current behaviour unless it says otherwise. The outline's six decisions (`explorations/reviews/fortress-repo-outline.md`) were taken at their defaults.

## The writers' points

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`

- In "When to explore", the sentence "The curator settles the question after research." says more than `exploring.md`, "The choices that are yours", which lets the agent make a choice that changes one area only, no line of the model and no decision, and can be undone. So a gap that meets those four conditions is the agent's choice in one file and the curator's in the other. I left the sentence unchanged. Options: (a) keep it as it is; (b) narrow it to "The curator settles a conflict, and new evidence against a decision of the curator, after research."; (c) cut it and leave the rule to `exploring.md`, which an agent loads when it switches. Option (a) keeps the current behaviour.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/records.md`

- The outline asks for the step `ledger.py check --rows FILE` before `ledger.py add`. That step does not work with the tool as it is. `check --rows` refuses a row with `?` in its number cell, and `add` requires exactly that `?`. `add` already runs the same template check before it writes. So the part says: write the row with `?`, run `add`, and `add` prints each broken rule and writes nothing. Alternatives: (a) keep the part as written, which is the current behaviour; (b) change `check --rows` to accept a `?` number cell, then put the step back. The outline also asks exploring.md's step 7 to check a report row with `check --rows`. Such a row fails the same way unless it carries a real row number.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/specification.md`

- The rule "quote each sentence of the specification that your change makes false" moves from specification.md to records.md's list of what every report holds. Its meaning stays the same: it already said "your change", and the script's REPORT.md paragraph asks it of every change. But in practice it now reaches workers who change code and never load specification.md. That is the case it exists for: batch 9's blocking finding was a change to walk that made an Appendix I effect false. Alternatives: (a) move it, as proposed; (b) keep it in specification.md, where only a worker in the specification area reads it. Option (b) keeps the current behaviour.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/gate.md`

- Step 3 runs the library order only after a build that started the caches again. The implementation's stamp covers `ProjectFortress/build/`, `third_party/`, `bin/` and `default_repository/configuration` (`build.xml`, `implementationFingerprint`), not `Library/` or `LibraryBuiltin/`. Compiling a program never recompiles a library component already in the cache (`build-and-caches.md`; `build-efficiency.md` 8.1). So suppose a gated tree changes one of the five compiled-library components and no Java. Then the caches are kept, and the atomic runs and the ladder copies run on the old library jars. A changed library body gives no warning; a changed api gives a false red (`NoSuchMethodError`). The suites are not affected, because they compile the library in private caches. Alternatives: (a) keep step 3 as it is; (b) also run the library order when `git diff` since the gated commit touches `LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.*`, `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.*` or `Library/Compiler*`; (c) run it in every gate, as the workflow script still does, at about 100 to 110 s of about 25 minutes. Option (a) keeps the current behaviour. The writer would choose (c), as the simplest rule with no hole.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/exploring.md`

- `ledger.py check --rows` counts the `?` in the number cell as a broken rule (ledger.py:525-526), but `add` requires that `?` (:757-758). So step 7 now adds a rule: correct the row until the check names no other rule. Alternatives: (a) keep this sentence; (b) change the tool so that `check --rows` accepts `?`, and drop the sentence. The outline also puts `check --rows FILE` before `add` in records.md. That step is redundant: `add` already runs the same lint (`template_row`, :584-590, called at :766) and prints each broken rule. It would also fail every time on the `?` that `add` needs. The check is needed only where no `add` follows, which is exploring.md's step 7.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/toolchain.md`

- A possible new rule. The preparser (`parser/preparser/`) and the import collector (`parser/import_collector/`) are two more Rats! parsers, each with its own `Compilation` and `Symbol` modules. The import collector's two are near copies of the main grammar's (`Compilation.rats` has 413 lines against 417; `Symbol.rats` differs in about 118 diff lines). The preparser's two are smaller variants. The part's copy rule names only the template parser. Alternatives: (a) keep the rule as it is until a worker meets such a change; (b) extend it: "If you change `Compilation.rats` or `Symbol.rats`, check the modules of the same name in `preparser/` and `import_collector/` too." Option (a) keeps the current behaviour. Not checked: whether a change to the main modules ever needs a matching change in those two parsers.

### `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/tests-running.md`

- The rule "Run one suite at a time in a tree" names only the two suites. The line "For a shared phase ... or the parser, run both" asks for `ant testQuick` and `ant testSystem`, and an agent may run the two at once. The two targets clash in three ways. `testSystem` and `testFast` delete all of `ProjectFortress/test-caches` when they start (`build.xml:1186`, `:1429`), which includes the folders of testQuick's tracks. Every test target deletes `ProjectFortress/test-tmp` when it ends (for example `:1125`, `:1436`), and the other target's JVMs use that folder as their temporary directory. Both targets run `ant compileAll` in one tree at the same time. Alternatives: (a) widen the rule to "Run one `ant` test target at a time in a tree, because each deletes the `test-caches` or `test-tmp` that another uses"; (b) leave the rule as it is, and write "run both, one after the other" in the shared-phase line; (c) leave both lines as they are. Option (c) keeps the current behaviour.
- The whole-suite rule is unclear for an edit of a parser grammar (`parser/*.rats`). The condition at its top names "the Java or Scala of the checker, of walk or of a phase that both paths share", which a `.rats` edit is not. Read that way, the edit falls under "every other change", so the agent runs only its own tests. The line below it says "For a shared phase ... or the parser, run both". Alternatives: (a) add "or a parser grammar" to the condition, so that a grammar edit runs testQuick and testSystem; (b) read "the parser" as its Java only, and write that a grammar edit runs only your own tests; (c) leave the text as it is. Option (c) keeps the current text, and most readers would then follow the parser line and run both.

## The fixer's point

- `SKILL.md`, the term "gate": its definition now ends "when a brief asks for it". The default taken: the wording as the fixer left it.

## The approved parts compared with the versions he approved

A Fable reviewer compared the three parts he approved (at `c69504e17`) with their rewritten versions and wrote a synthesis where it found a regression.

- `references/build-and-caches.md`: synthesized. Kept the new version almost whole: the glossary (tree with its default, library order, DSL grammar, parser directory), "Setting up each call" moved to the top with the install line and the tree-root note, the corrected DSL-grammar fact (ForUse.fss is gated: SyntaxAbstractionJUTest in the misc track), and the cuts of facts that SKILL.md or another section states once (walk interprets, fortress compile type-checks, the class loader, the global.map bullet, test targets build first, who needs no library order). All checked against the sources or the tree. One regression fixed: the rewritten DSL-grammar sentence ended "and so do the ungated tests in that folder" right after naming explorations/apl/, so "that folder" read as the APL folder; the approved version named ProjectFortress/syntax_abstraction_tests/ unambiguously. Rewrote it as "The ungated tests beside it import one, and so do the APL experiments under explorations/apl/", which keeps the new fact (ForUse.fss) and the approved clarity.
- `references/tests-writing.md`: synthesized. Kept the new version's gains: the glossary, the PASS line in the template, library_tests/ against the interpreter's library, the pair explained at the XXX prefix, item 2 bound to a deferred defect, item 3's walk-crash case, step 2 pointing to worktrees.md "Running the old code" (which covers walk through the base build's harness-one.sh, which old-fortress.sh alone did not), the test with no fix, the compile refusal's key, the wall pointed to compiler.md, the run-time example in the second run, promotion with committing.md's git mv commit and the pair's three files. Two regressions fixed by synthesis: (1) the run rule had been merged into one sentence with three nested "if" clauses; restored the approved two sentences (principle 5: one instruction per sentence), same meaning. (2) The approved line on prose edits was moved to specification.md, but SKILL.md still ends its test-first rule with "An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (references/tests-writing.md)", so the pointer landed on nothing; added one routing sentence: "An edit of prose in Specification/ or Documentation/ has no test. Check it as specification.md, \"Changing the text: the revision form\", says." It names the part and section that hold the rule rather than repeating it.
- `references/tests-running.md`: kept. No change. Every difference from the approved version is as good or better and checked: the compiler track as the longest (suites-at-four-threads.md: 525.8 s against othercompiler's 366.4 s), testSystem in 2 to 4 minutes (1:52 to 4:03 across the landed gate summaries), the verdict in the line before Total time: (ant's last line is Total time), every ant test target building first stated once at the suites, OverloadRewriter as a shared phase (PhaseOrder.java) and OverloadSet with the code generator (it imports codegen and ASM), DSL grammars except ForUse.fss, the direct run with -debug stacktrace from ProjectFortress/ (sourced in Shell.java and Debug.java), seed-or-build pointed to worktrees.md. The cuts (track caches reason moved to the caches bullet, "once for each code state" shortened to "once, after your last edit of code", "a change of tests, prose or records only" covered by "every other change", the testOnly/track build-first and 9-minute lines covered elsewhere in the part) lose no knowledge the part or SKILL.md does not still state.

content.content:
- Trigger: the cache comment (2026-10-05 04:09) and then the opening's sentences. The "team" sentence took six coordinator rewrites on one thread. The walk sentence took seven across four threads, in two hours.
- Became: on 2026-10-05 05:52 he said "Please rewrite the section since you already know it's wrong. I don't want to be doing line level editing when you can come up with a good version." The build section was rewritten whole. The POSITIONS entry on the skills gained: a comment marks a problem area, and the fix is made at the level of its paragraph or section.

**M2. A separate writer.**

- Trigger: the coordinator's context (about 600K tokens, full of the record in earlier models' shorthand) wrote worse sentences. 2026-10-05 05:02: "Do I need to compact you, to recover your writing skills?" and 05:09 "That's it, I've had it with you." He compacted it. He asked for a backup: a writer from a clean context, so that the coordinator briefs and does not interpret his words.
- Became: 2026-10-06 19:15, a writer for the whole skill. 2026-10-07 03:56, a standing writer with a standing order: ASD-STE100, define a term before use, state rules positively, do not take the register of what you read. His word: the writer's job is "that of an exorcist", exorcising "the sins of earlier models, speaking in tongues". 2026-10-08 04:26, a headless session on the one-hour prompt cache (`explorations/coordinator/tools/skill-writer.sh`, brief in `skill-writer-brief.md`). He accepted the double cost of writing the cache ("I think it would be worth it"). 2026-10-08 08:19: past one hour, start a fresh writer. The coordinator makes no skill edit itself.

**M3. Archaeology of what workers actually did.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-05 05:47, after the cache comment: "when we have discovered a better way to do something, but most of the agents are working around some issue, we need to encode the best practice into the skill". This "requires a bit more data-driven approach".
- Became: a rule in the POSITIONS entry (where a practice is in question, an archaeology worker checks). Then: the worker-decisions archaeology (2026-10-07) for the conflict procedure; the pre-training quiz (a fresh session describes Fortress from its training alone, and the answers are graded) and the distillation audit (a reader compares the notes with the skill's parts and lists what daily work needs and the parts lack), both 2026-10-08; the ledger archaeology, the context study (what batch 10's workers read before their first edit) and the testing-practices archaeology, all 2026-10-08. He also asked the coordinator to check INDEX for earlier notes before a launch: "Didn't we run that once already?" (2026-10-08 11:29).

**M4. A cold read, and routing.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-05 05:54, he asked for a fresh worker "specifically with the task of flagging consequences of certain descriptions that are unclear to them because they lack the correct contents", with scenarios that contain traps.
- Became: the cold read of `fortress-repo` by readers given only the skill. It found rules that could send an agent wrong, such as the one on the script `env.sh`, which deletes files that running jobs use. They were fixed the same day. He then saw that testing traps is pointless "if they don't know when to trigger those". The skill `remote-container` was split by who needs it. What every worker needs of a Claude Code session (the Bash timeout, long commands, waits) moved to `session.md` in `fortress-repo`. The routing descriptions were optimized again. He asked whether a rename was needed ("I don't want to trigger another round of rename cascade") before he accepted one.

**M5. A rename at the source: "stop" to "points to report".**

- Trigger: 2026-10-06 17:13: the word "stop" read as a condition that stops the worker. His second comment: the coordinator had quoted a POSITIONS title as his own words. "That is definitely not my language."
- Became: the word is gone from `fortress-repo` and the `coordinator` skill. The replacement is "points to report": the kinds of change or finding that a brief names for his review. The batch script and the record still say "stop". That edit is owed with the next script edit. POSITIONS now says that a bold title is the record's handle, never quoted to him as his words.

**M6. The boundary between a skill and the workflow.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-06 18:02, on a line that named the checker count. "We are done with the skill we are going back to optimizing the workflow."
- Became: the part on measurements left `fortress-repo`. The `coordinator` skill names them and points to the workflow script. The role-neutral rule (lens 4) stands.

**M7. From comment by comment to lenses.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-06 19:13: "I do not want to go comment by comment because I think we were touching each every line." He asked for an estimate and for a characterization of what he was doing. The coordinator estimated about 4 hours for the 8K characters of `SKILL.md` and 60 hours or more for the rest at that pace.
- Became: the lenses note, and a writer pass over every part (about 366K tokens, by the coordinator's count). The POSITIONS entry says his review goes by the lenses, applied to a whole skill at once and then read by him. A fault of that pass: it dropped two defaults that decide what an agent does when its brief is silent. The coordinator restored them the same evening. A cut that removes a default changes meaning.

**M8. Register is structure.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-05 06:41 (tone), then 2026-10-07 03:37 ("spaghetti").
- Became: the register in POSITIONS, the writer's standing order, and the two modes with `exploring.md`. His words (2026-10-07 04:01): "it is not just a tone … a structural rewrite because you need to establish the term and reorder the things".

**M9. The conflict procedure and the executive assistant.**

- Trigger: 2026-10-07 02:54, a proposed wording for "two sources disagree" that did not read like ASD-STE100 to him. He explained what a worker should do in each situation and asked what the batch workers actually did.
- Became: the worker-decisions archaeology. The four conditions for a worker's own choice. The form of a decision not taken. On 2026-10-07 04:52, three minor questions from the writer: "stop bothering me with bullshit … Can't you just make good judgment on those?" POSITIONS now says the coordinator settles a writer's minor decisions from the record, as his executive assistant. He is asked only where a rule would change its meaning or a new rule would enter.

**M10. A problem found while reading, recorded and not fixed in the skill.**
